title: A Divided Church and the Message of the Cross
summary: Paul greets the Corinthian church as God's holy people and thanks God for the gifts they have received. He then confronts the quarrels he has heard about, as members line up behind Paul, Apollos, Cephas, or Christ. He answers that Christ is not divided and that the message of the crucified Christ, foolish and weak in the world's eyes, is God's power and wisdom, as the humble social makeup of the church itself shows.
story: Paul had founded the church in Corinth a few years earlier, during a stay of about eighteen months described in Acts 18. After he left, the gifted teacher Apollos worked there, and other leaders may have visited. Now Paul is in Ephesus, and reports have reached him that the church is splintering. This chapter opens the first major section of the letter (1:10-4:21), which deals with those divisions. Paul does not start with church politics. He starts with the cross, because he sees the factions as a symptom of a deeper problem: the church has absorbed its city's love of status, eloquence, and wisdom, and forgotten the shape of the gospel that created it.
historical:
Corinth had been refounded as a Roman colony by Julius Caesar in 44 BC, after the old Greek city was destroyed in 146 BC. By the 50s AD it was a busy commercial center and the capital of the province of Achaia, a place where freed slaves and merchants could rise in wealth and status. Paul arrived around AD 50 and was brought before the governor Gallio, whose term an inscription from Delphi dates to around AD 51 to 52 (Acts 18:12). He wrote this letter from Ephesus a few years later, most likely around AD 53 to 55.

Several people in this chapter appear elsewhere. Sosthenes may be the synagogue ruler beaten in Corinth in Acts 18:17, though the identification is uncertain. Crispus was the synagogue ruler who believed with his household (Acts 18:8). Gaius may be the host Paul mentions in Romans 16:23. Apollos was a learned Jew from Alexandria in Egypt, powerful in the Scriptures, who taught in Corinth after Paul left (Acts 18:24-28). Cephas is the Aramaic form of the name Peter; whether Peter himself had visited Corinth or some members simply claimed his authority is unknown. Chloe's household probably refers to her slaves or employees who traveled on business between Corinth and Ephesus.
cultural:
Greek and Roman cities prized rhetoric, the art of persuasive public speaking. Orators and traveling teachers, often called sophists, gathered students and admirers, and people attached themselves to favorite speakers much as fans follow celebrities. Eloquence and polished presentation were signs of education and status. When the Corinthians said "I follow Paul" or "I follow Apollos", they may have been treating Christian leaders like competing teachers. Apollos, with his Alexandrian learning and eloquence, may have seemed more impressive than Paul.

The cross, meanwhile, was the most shameful form of death in the Roman world, reserved mainly for slaves, rebels, and the lowest criminals. Respectable Romans avoided even speaking of it. A graffito found on the Palatine Hill in Rome, usually dated to the second or third century, mocks a Christian named Alexamenos for worshiping a crucified figure with a donkey's head. To proclaim a crucified man as Lord and as the wisdom of God was, for Greeks, absurd, and for Jews, who read in Deuteronomy 21:23 that one hung on a tree is under God's curse, deeply offensive. Paul does not soften that offense. He makes it the center of his message.
literary: The chapter follows the pattern of an ancient letter: sender and recipients (verses 1-2), a greeting (verse 3), and a thanksgiving (verses 4-9). The thanksgiving quietly introduces themes the letter will address: speech, knowledge, spiritual gifts, and waiting for the day of Christ. Verse 10 states the purpose of the first section, an appeal for unity. Paul then argues with sharp rhetorical questions ("Is Christ divided? Was Paul crucified for you?"). Verses 18 to 25 are built on paired contrasts: foolishness and power, the perishing and the saved, Jews and Greeks, signs and wisdom, weakness and strength. Verses 26 to 31 apply the argument to the Corinthians themselves, using a triple "not many" and a triple "God chose". Paul closes with a quotation from Jeremiah 9:24.

outline.t: Greeting to the church of God in Corinth
The foolishness and power of the cross
God chose the lowly: boast in the Lord

doctrines.note: The message of the cross is the power of God for those being saved. Christ has become for believers wisdom from God, righteousness, holiness, and redemption, so everything they have comes from his death and belongs to him.

The church belongs to God and is joined to all who call on the name of the Lord everywhere. It cannot be divided into parties loyal to leaders, because Christ is not divided and no leader was crucified for it.
God's wisdom is revealed in what the world counts foolish: a crucified Messiah. This does not reject thinking, but it overturns the claim that human wisdom, left to itself, can find its way to God.

words.note: Schisma, a tear or split, the source of the English word schism. It was used for a tear in cloth (Mark 2:21) and for divisions of opinion in a crowd (John 7:43). In verse 10 it describes the factions within the church. Paul treats them as a tear in something that should be whole.

Moria, foolishness, from which English gets the word moron. It appears three times in this chapter. Paul uses it for how the message of the cross looks to those who are perishing and to Greeks, and then turns the word around: the foolishness of God is wiser than human wisdom.

Sophia, wisdom. It appears eight times in this chapter and is central to the first four chapters of the letter. Paul contrasts the wisdom of the world, meaning human cleverness, eloquence, and status, with the wisdom of God revealed in the cross. He does not reject wisdom as such; he says Christ has become wisdom from God for believers.

Kauchaomai, to boast or take pride in. Boasting was a normal part of public life in Corinth, where people advertised their achievements and connections. Paul says God chose the lowly so that no one may boast before him, and quotes Jeremiah: the one who boasts should boast in the Lord.

christ: This chapter presents Christ crucified as the heart of the gospel. Paul does not preach Christ in spite of the cross but Christ as the crucified one, and he names that crucified Christ "the power of God and the wisdom of God" (verse 24). The title recalls Israel's wisdom tradition, in which wisdom was with God at creation (Proverbs 8), and suggests that what Israel longed to know of God's wisdom has now appeared in a person. Christ has become for believers wisdom, righteousness, holiness, and redemption (verse 30), gathering the whole of salvation into himself. Paul also calls him "our Lord Jesus Christ, their Lord and ours" (verse 2) and speaks of the day of our Lord Jesus Christ (verse 8), borrowing the Old Testament language of the day of the Lord. The church is called into fellowship with the Son, which is why divisions around human leaders make no sense.

hard.q: Is Paul against intellectual thought and careful argument?
hard.a:
Paul's contrast between God's wisdom and the world's wisdom has sometimes been read as a rejection of learning, reason, or philosophy. The chapter itself resists that reading. Paul is a skilled thinker whose letter is full of careful argument, and he calls Christ the wisdom of God. What he rejects is the wisdom of this age as a path to God and as a source of status: the belief that clever people can reach God through their own brilliance, and the habit of ranking people by eloquence and education.

Christians have handled this tension in different ways. Some, like the early writer Tertullian, stressed the gap between Athens and Jerusalem, meaning Greek philosophy and Christian faith. Others, like Augustine and Thomas Aquinas, used philosophy extensively in the service of faith. Most Christian traditions agree that reason is a gift of God that serves faith well, but that the gospel cannot be reduced to or discovered by human wisdom alone. The cross stands as a standing critique of any intellectual system, religious or secular, that makes itself the measure of truth.

questions: Where do you see Christians lining up behind favorite leaders, teachers, or movements today? What does Paul's question "Is Christ divided?" say to that?
The Corinthians were not many wise, powerful, or noble by human standards. How does God's choice of the lowly challenge the way churches value people?
What in the message of the cross still seems foolish or offensive to people today, and why?
